[If her sons'] conception was not in sanctity, but their birth was in sanctity, they may perform either chalitzah or yibbum, but they are liable on account of "the wife of one's brother." [If] their conception was in sanctity and their birth was in sanctity, behold, they are like an Israelite in every respect.

Five women whose newborns got mixed up, and they grew up mixed up, and they married women and [one of them] died, [and] some of them were brothers and some of them were not brothers: The brothers perform chalitzah, [and] those that were not brothers perform yibbum. [If] some of them were priests and some of them were not priests, the priests perform chalitzah, and those that were not priests perform yibbum. [If] some of them were brothers and some of them were priests, they [all] perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum. [If] there is a doubt whether [the yevama] is his mother, or a doubt whether she is his daughter, or a doubt whether she is his sister, they perform [all] chalitzah and do not perform yibbum. This is the general rule: In all [situations of] doubt involving a yevama, they perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum.

How is it that a man may [come to] perform chalitzah with his own mother due to uncertainty? His mother and another woman had two male offspring (i.e., one each), and they went back and gave birth to two [more] male offspring in while in hiding. The first two [offspring] stood up, [and] this one took the mother of that one [as a wife], and that one took the mother of this one [as a wife], and he died without offspring. [In this scenario,] this one performs chalitzah with both of them, and that one performs chalitzah with both of them. It turns out that a man may perform chalitzah with his own mother due to uncertainty. § How is it that a man may [come to] perform chalitzah with his own sister due to uncertainty? His mother and another woman had two female offspring, and they went back and gave birth to two [more] female offspring while in hiding, and they got married to two brothers from the father's side but not from the mother's side, and they died without offspring. [In this scenario,] this one performs chalitzah on both of them. It turns out that this man performs chalitzah with his own sister due to uncertainty.  § How is it that a man may [come to] perform chalitzah with his own daughter due to uncertainty? His wife and another woman gave birth to two female offspring while in hiding, and they got married to two brothers from the father's side but not from the mother's side, and they died without offspring. [In this scenario,] he performs chalitzah on both of them. It turns out that this man performs chalitzah with his own daughter due to uncertainty.

A priestess whose offspring were mixed up with the offspring of her maidservant: They may not eat from that which is separated from most holy consecrated things [of the priesthood], for servants of the priesthood may not eat from that which is separated from most holy consecrated things, but they may eat from that which is separated from consecrated things of lesser holiness, from which the servants of the priesthood may eat. Both of them may go out to the threshing floor and take one portion [between themselves], for the servant [of a priest] is not given [a portion] unless his master was with him. Rabbi Yosei says, I could say to him, "If it is with the authority of my master, a priest, I give myself [a portion] with the authority of my master, and if not, I give myself with my own authority." [If] the mixed-up offspring grew up an each one freed the other, they may not eat from that which is separated from consecrated things of lesser holiness, for non-priests may not eat from them. Rabbi Yehuda says, the terumah is sold and purchased with its value in chullin, for anyone who cannot eat from the consecrated things of others may not eat from his own consecrated things.

Anyone who did not wait three months after [the death of] her husband, and got married and gave birth, and it is not known [which husband is the father], if he is presumptively [the offspring] of the first, behold, he is [deemed to be] the offspring of the first; [and] if he is presumptively [the offspring] of the second, behold, he is [deemed to be] the offspring of the second. [If there is] a doubt [whether the offspring is] a ninth-month (i.e., full-term) child of the first or a seven-month child of the last, [and] he strikes this one and goes back and strikes that one, [or] curses this one and goes back and curses that one, behold, he is exempt [from the death penalty]. [If] he strikes both of them at one time, he is liable. Rabbi Yehuda says, one who strikes his father and another man at one time is exempt, [but] one who curses his father and another man at one time is liable. [If] she had children from the first one and children from the second one, they (i.e., the brothers of the deceased husbands) perform neither chalitzah nor yibbum (contra Yevamot 11:7 ("they perform chalitzah but not yibbum")). And similarly, he neither performs chalitzah nor yibbum on them. [If] he had brothers from the first and brothers from the second that are not from the same mother, he performs chalitzah or yibbum on them (i.e., the wives of his deceased half-brothers). And so too with him; they (i.e., his half brothers) may perform chalitzah or yibbum [on his wives after his death].

A woman about whom a bad name (i.e., regarding promiscuity) has come out: Her offspring are deemed fit, because they are presumed to be of her husband. Rabbi Yehuda says, [if] both of them (i.e., her husband and her alleged paramour) are from the same [priestly] patrilinear family, [the doubtful offspring] are given one [priestly] portion.

The commandment of chalitzah must be performed before three [individuals acting as judges], as long as they know how to recite [the relevant verses]. Rabbi Yehuda says, before five. Said Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, it so happened that [there was a woman] who performed chalitzah before only Rabbi Yishmael, at night.

[If] she performed chalitzah with a sandal that opened up but can [still] hold most of the foot, with a shoe that became separated and [still] covers most of the foot, with a sandal of bamboo (sha'am), with a sandal of hemp, with a stocking, with a prosthetic leg, with a leg-blanket (i.e., which is used by an amputee), with a felt-shoe of leather, and one who performs chalitzah with an adult man, whether standing or sitting or leaning, [and] one who performs chalitzah from [a yavam who is] a blind man -- [in all these cases,] her chalitzah is valid. With a sandal that opened up and does not hold most of the foot, with a shoe that became separated does not cover most of the foot, with a hand-blanket, with [a felt-shoe] of cloth, and one who performs chalitzah form [a yavam who is] a minor -- ]in all these cases,] her chalitzah is disqualified. Said Rabbi Yehuda, if Rabbi Eliezer would have seen a wooden sandal from nowadays, he would have said about it, "Behold, it is like [any other] sandal in every respect." Said Rabbi Shimon*in the Bavli, Yevamot 102a:8-9, the following anecdote is attributed to Rabbi Yosei, I came across an old man from Netzivin, and I said to him, "Did you ever happen to know Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira?" He said to me, "Yes, and he used to frequent my table." I said to him, "Did you ever see him perform (i.e., officiate over) a chalitzah in your lifetime?" He said to me, "Yes." I said to him, "With what did you see him, with a shoe or a sandal?" He said to me, "And who would perform chalitzah with a shoe?!" I said to him, "If so, why did Rabbi Meir see fit to say that chalitzah may be performed with a shoe?" Rabbi Ya'akov says in his name, Rabbi Meir [actually] was in agreement that chalitzah may not be performed with a shoe.

A minor girl who performed chalitzah must perform chalitzah [again] once she reaches adulthood. [If] she did not perform chalitzah [as a minor], her chalitzah [as an adult] is disqualified, the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And the Sages say, if she did not perform chalitzah [as a minor], her chalitzah [as an adult] is valid. § [If] the straps of his shoe or sandal slipped out, or if the majority of the of the shoe covering his foot slipped out, her chalitzah is disqualified, [but] if he wanted to return [to her], she may not return.  [If] she performed chalitzah, but did not spit [at him], or did not recite the verse (see Deut. 25:9), her chalitzah is valid, [and] if he wanted to return [to her], he may not return. [If] she spit but did not recite the verse or remove the shoe, [her] chalitzah is disqualified. [If] she recited the verse but did not spit or remove the shoe, she has not done anything, and he may return [to her].

A mistaken chalitzah is [nonetheless] valid. [If] he removed his shoe for her, [and] he intended [that it be for chalitzah] and she did not intend it, [or] she intends it and he did not intend it, her chalitzah is disqualified. A chalitzah administered by a Jewish court is valid, [but] by a court of idolaters is invalid. [But in regards to] a court of idolaters, [if] they were to beat him and say to him, "Do what Rabbi So-and-So tells you to do," [the chalitzah is valid].

[The judges] may perform (i.e., officiate over) chalitzah on a woman even if they don't know her. They may perform miyun even if they don't know her. A woman who said, "I did chalitzah," must bring proof to support her words. [If she said] "I did miyun," she must bring proof to support her words.

Originally they would write the bill of chalitzah [as follows]: "[So-and-so] came forward before [the court] and she removed the shoe from his right foot, [and] she spat before him, and she said (Deut. 25:9), 'Such should befall, etc.'" Rabbi Shimon says in the name of Rabbi Akiva, [the failure] to remove the shoe prevents [the chalitzah from taking effect], but [the failure] to spit does not prevent. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, since [the brother] did not desire to establish a name for his brother in Israel, he comes and take a [new] name in exchange for his name, [as it says,] "And his name in Israel shall be called, etc."

The commandment [to recite the declaration stated in Deut. 25:8] is incumbent upon the judges, not upon the the students [who attend the court sessions]. Rabbi Yehuda says, the commandment is incumbent upon all those who stand [in attendance] to say, "The one stripped of the shoe, the one stripped of the shoe, the one stripped of the shoe." Said Rabbi Yehuda, it once happened that we were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, and he said to us, "Answer, all of you, 'The one stripped of the shoe, the one stripped of the shoe.'"

Originally they would write documents of miyun (i.e., the declaration of refusal by a minor girl), "She is not a comfort to him, and she is not a companion to him, and she does not desire to be married to him." Beit Hillel say, [the declaration may be made either] before the court or not before the court (Yevamot 13:1), as long as there are three [witnesses]. Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon say, even before two. How is the commandment of miyun [carried out]? She says, "I do not desire so-and-so as my husband," [or] "I do not desire the betrothal with which my mother or my brothers caused me to be betrothed." Even if she is seated in the palanquin (i.e., being conducted to her husband's house) and went to whoever arranged her betrothal, and stated in front of him, "I do not desire so-and-so as my husband," there is no declaration of refusal that is greater than that. Rabbi Yehuda says, even if she went to take away a certain purchase from a shopkeeper, and she said in front of him, "I do not desire so-and-so as my husband," there is no declaration of refusal that is greater than that. Rabbi Yehuda said even more than that: Even if guests are reclining [at her wedding feast], and she said in front of them, "I do not desire so-and-so as my husband," there is no declaration of refusal greater than that. [As to] a minor girl who became betrothed on her own and got married of her own during the lifetime of her father, her betrothal is not a [valid] betrothal, and her marriage is not a [valid] marriage.

[A minor girl] who performed miyun with a man: She does not have [a right to the payments enumerated in] her marriage contract. [If] he gave her a divorce document, she does have her marriage contract. Rabbi Eliezer says, the actions of a minor are a nullity. [Her husband] has no right to the items she finds, nor to [her earnings derived from] the work of her hands, nor to annul her vows, nor does he inherit her, and [if he is a priest] he may not contract impurity through her [corpse], and she is not like a wife in any respect; rather, she may go out from [her marriage to] him with miyun. Rabbi Yehoshua says, he does have a right to the items she finds, and to [her earnings derived from] the work of her hands, and to annul her vows, and he does inherit her, and [if he is a priest] he may contract impurity through her [corpse], and behold, she is like a wife in every respect except that she goes out from [her marriage to] him with miyun (i.e., instead of with a divorce document). Said Rabbi Yishmael: I went back over all the measures (i.e., the opinions) of all the Sages, and I didn't find any man whose applied a consistent measure to a minor girl except for Rabbi Eliezer, and I prefer his words to the words of Rabbi Yehoshua, for Rabbi Eliezer is consistent with his measures, and Rabbi Yishmael is inconsistent.*In the Bavli (Yevamot 108a:14), this statement is attributed to Rebbi. The Gemara comments that the inconsistency of Rabbi Yehoshua is that, if a minor girl is indeed like a wife in every respect, she should require a divorce document rather than miyun.

[A minor girl] who performed miyun with a man and returned to him and he died: She is subject to either chalitzah or yibbum. [If] he divorced her (i.e., while she was still a minor) and she returned to him, she is subject to either chalitzah or yibbum. Rabbi Eliezer says, she is subject to chalitzah but not yibbum because she was forbidden to him for a period of time. The Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer with regards to a minor whose father married her off, and he divorced her, and she returned to him and he died, that she is subject to chalitzah but not yibbum, since she was forbidden to her for a period of time, because her divorce [is considered] a full-fledged divorce, and her return is not a full-fledged return.*A father is not permitted to marry his minor daughter off a second time, and she lacks the capacity to enter into marriage herself while she is a minor. (See Ketubot 73b:16.) When do these words apply? Whenever he divorced her as a minor girl, and she returned to him as a minor, but [if] he divorced her as a minor and she returned to him as an adult, or if he divorced her as a minor and she returned to him as a minor and grew up under him (i.e., supported by him), and he died, she is subject to either chalitzah or yibbum. Rabbi Eliezer says, she is subject to chalitzah but not yibbum because she was forbidden to him for a period of time.

This is the general rule: A divorce document after miyun,  it is forbidden to return to him. Miyun after a divorce document, it is permitted to return to him. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel and Rabbi Yishmael b'Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karcha say: Either this way or that way, since she went out from [her marriage to] him with a divorce document, it is forbidden to return to him. It once happened that there was a certain [minor girl] who got married as an orphan, and she got divorced, and she returned to him, and [then] performed miyun with him, and got married to another man, and he died, and they came and asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, what is her status? May she return to her first husband? And he said to them, either this way or that way, since she went out from [her marriage to] him with a divorce document, she is forbidden to return to him.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, if she performs miyun, her miyun is valid. If not, she waits until she reaches adulthood and performs chalitzah, and this one goes out on account of [the prohibition against marrying] "his wife's sister." § Two brothers who married two orphans -- a minor girl and a deaf-mute. [If] the husband of the minor girl dies, the deaf-mute goes out with a divorce document, and the minor girl waits until she reaches adulthood and performs chalitzah. [If] the husband of the deaf-mute dies, the minor girl goes out with a divorce document, and the deaf-mute is forbidden forever [to remarry], but if one does come upon her, she goes out with a divorce document and she is released [to marry another man].

One who was married to two minor orphan girls and died, [and] a yavam came upon the first one, and returned and came upon the second one: Both of them are forbidden to him. And so too with two female deaf-mutes. A minor girl and a female deaf-mute: [If] the yavam came upon the minor, and returned and came upon the deaf-mute, or his brother came upon the deaf-mute, both of them are forbidden to him. The deaf-mute goes out with a divorce document and the minor goes out with a divorce document and chalitzah.

[One who was married to] a mentally sound [woman] and to a deaf-mute [and died], [and] a yavam came upon the mentally sound one, and returned and came upon the deaf-mute, or his brother came upon the deaf-mute: They are both forbidden to him (i.e., the yavam). The deaf-mute goes out with a divorce document [and] the one who is mentally sound goes out with a divorce document and chalitzah. [One who was married to] an adult woman and a minor girl [and died], [and] a yavam came upon the adult woman and returned and came upon the minor girl, or his brother came upon the minor girl: They are both forbidden to him.  The minor girl goes out with a divorce document, [and] the adult woman goes out with a divorce document and chalitzah. Rabbi Eliezer says,  in all of these cases, they instruct the minor girl to make a declaration of refusal against him (Yevamot 13:7).

A yevama who within 30 days [after yibbum] said, "He has not had intercourse with me,"*lit., "There has been no intercourse with me"; the Hebrew is phrased in the passive tense ("lo niv'alti") whether [the yavam] said, "I did have intercourse [with her]," or whether he said, "I did not have intercourse [with her]," they force him to give her chalitzah. [If she made that statement] after thirty days, they request from him that he perform chalitzah on her. [If] she says, "He has had intercourse with me," and he says, "I did not have intercourse [with her]," behold, this one goes out with a divorce document. [If] he says, "I had intercourse [with her]," and she says, "He did not have intercourse with me," even if he returned and said, "I did not have intercourse [with her]," behold, this one goes out with a divorce document. Rabbi Yehuda says, [if] she vowed that she would never have yibbum performed on her, even [if she made the vow] during the lifetime of her husband, they request from him that he perform chalitzah on her.

How does [a deaf mute] take her out [from the marriage] with gestures (Yevamot 14:1)? He gestures and gives her divorce document to her. A mentally sound woman [who is married] to a mentally sound man, and he has a mentally sound brother; [or] a mentally sound woman [who is married] to a deaf-mute, and he has a mentally sound brother: [The brother] may perform either chalitzah or yibbum. A mentally sound woman [who is married] to a mentally sound man, and he has a deaf-mute brother: [The brother] must marry her and he may never divorce her. A mentally sound woman [who is married] to a deaf-mute, and he has a deaf-mute brother; a female deaf-mute [who is married] to a mentally sound man, and he has a mentally sound brother; a female deaf mute [who is married] to a mentally sound man, and he has a deaf-mute brother; a female deaf-mute [who is married] to a deaf-mute and he has a mentally sound brother; [or] a female deaf-mute [who is married] to a deaf-mute and he has a deaf-mute brother: [The brother] must marry her, [and] if he wants to take her out [from the marriage], he takes her out, and if he wants to remain with her, he remains with her.

Two deaf-mute brothers who married two mentally sound sisters, or two deaf-mute sisters, or two sisters, one mentally sound and one deaf-mute; and so too two deaf-mute sisters who got married to two mentally sound brothers, or to two deaf-mute brothers, or to two brothers, one mentally sound and one deaf-mute; and so too two brothers, one mentally sound and one deaf-mute, who married two sisters, one mentally sound and one deaf-mute, the mentally sound [sister] to the mentally sound [brother], and the deaf-mute [sister] to the deaf-mute [brother]: Neither chalitzah nor yibbum applies here; rather, his wife (i.e., the deceased brother's wife) remains with him. The other one goes out on account of [the prohibition against marrying] "a woman and her sister." [If] they were unrelated, he must marry her, [and] if he wants to take her out [from the marriage], he takes her out, and if he wants to remain with her, he remains with her.

A woman who said, "My husband divorced me," [or] "My yavam subjected me to chalitzah," [or] "My yavam performed yibbum on me and died": This one is not believed as to any of these [statements]. [As to] all those who are not believed to testify about her*להעידה (see Lieberman), she is also not believed to testify about them.

[If] one witness says, "He died," and one witness says, "He didn't die," [or] one woman says, "He died," and one woman says, "He didn't die," behold, [the man's wife] may not remarry. Rabbi Menachem b'Rabbi Yosei says, [if] one witness says, "He died," and one witness says, "He didn't die," and she remarried, and another witness came along and said, "He didn't die," behold, she is not sent out [from the subsequent marriage]*alt., "[if] one witness says, 'He died,' and she remarried, and [then] another witness came along and said, 'He didn't die,' she is not sent out" (Minchat Yitzchak); however, if at the beginning one witness says, "He died," and one witness says, "He didn't die," [or] one woman says, "He died," and one woman says, "He didn't die," even though she [subsequently] remarried, she is sent out. [If] one [woman] says, "He died," and two [women] say, "He did not die," behold, two women are like one man. Rabbi Nehemiah says, wherever the Sages validated the testimony of a woman like that of a man, the same [evidentiary rules apply to both]. Everything follows after [the majority of*אחר רוב (GR"A)] the testimony. Two women against one woman is like two [male] witnesses against one man. [But if] two say, "He died," and one hundred say "He didn't die," behold, the one hundred are [considered] like two witnesses.

[A man] betrothed one of five women, and he does not know which one he betrothed, and each and every one of them say, "He betrothed me" (Yevamot 15:7); [or] he purchased an item from [one of] five [sellers], and he does not know from which one he purchased it, and each and every one of them say, "He purchased it from me": Said Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva did not disagree regarding one who betrothed one of five women and he does not know which one he betrothed, that he leaves the ketubah payment between them all and departs. About what did they disagree? About one who had intercourse. And they did not disagree about one who purchased an item from [one of] five [sellers] and he does not know from which one he purchased it, that he leaves the payment for the item between them and departs. About what did they disagree? About one who stole. Rabbi Tarfon concedes that one who says to two people, "I stole a maneh (100 zuz) from one of you, and I don't know which one it was," or "One of your fathers deposited a maneh with me, and I don't know which one it was," he gives this one a maneh and that one a maneh, since he himself has admitted liability (see B.M. 3:3).

A woman whose husband traveled to lands overseas, and they came and said to her, "Your husband is dead," and he had a brother, and [the brother] performed yibbum on her, and died, and afterwards her husband returned: He is forbidden to her but permitted to her rival wives; he is forbidden to her but permitted to his brother's wife.

A woman who traveled with her husband to lands overseas, and she came back and said, "My husband is dead": She is permitted and her rival wife is forbidden. Rabbi Elazar*see Yevamot 16:2 says, since they were [previously] permitted to their yavams, they are [subsequently] permitted to any man.*Alternatively: "Rabbi Elazar says, since she was permitted, her rival wife was [also] permitted. [If] they had yibbum performed on them and their yavams died, they are forbidden to remarry. Rabbi Elazar says, since they were [previously] permitted to their yavams, they are [subsequently] permitted to any man." (MSS Erfurt/Vienna, Lieberman.)

[If a man had] two wives, one of whom had witnesses [to the death of her husband] and children, and the other of whom had neither witnesses nor children: Both of them are permitted [to marry]. § [A man who] fell into a pit of lions: They may not testify about him (i.e., his presumed death). Inside a fiery furnace, they may testify about him. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, he could have cauterized [his wounds] and survived.*Per Yevamot 120b:7, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar made this comment in connection with testifying about one who was seen being cut up (Yevamot 16:3).

[If] he fell into a pit that was full of snakes and scorpions [and does not emerge], they may testify about him. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says, they should be concerned lest he was a snake-charmer. [If] he fell into a vat of boiling oil or wine, they may testify about him. Rabbi Aha says, of oil, they may testify; but of wine, they may not testify about him. Eliezer ben Mahavai says, they may testify based on [identification by] a mole (i.e., a distinguishing mark on the skin). § [If the witness testifies,] "So-and-so is dead," "So-and-so has perished," "So-and-so has been killed," "So-and-so is no longer in this world," [or] "There is nothing left of him," his wife may remarry. --?-- they may not so testify about him.*The Tosefta is defective here. Minchat Bikkurim, citing the GR"A, would supply the following emendation: "'His ship sank in the sea,' they may not so testify about him."

[If] he fell into [a body of] water, whether it has an end (i.e., a visible shoreline) or whether it does not have an end, his wife is forbidden, the words of Rabbi Meir.*In the Mishnah (Yevamot 16:4), Rabbi Meir's opinion is given over as the stam Mishnah. And the Sages say, water that has an end, his wife is permitted, [and] water that has no end, his wife is forbidden, lest a wave have carried him and brought him up to dry land. Said Rabbi Akiva, once when I was traveling by sea, I saw a ship that sank in the sea, and I was in distress over a Torah scholar that was inside of it. And when I arrived at the country of Cappadocia, I saw him sit down and inquire before me regarding halacha. I said to him, "My son, how did you emerge from the sea?" He said to me*נם לי not גם לי ("Also to me") (see Lieberman), "A wave carried me to its fellow, and that one to its fellow, and that one to its fellow, until I reached dry land." I said, "How great are the words of the Sages, who used to say, 'Water that has an end, his wife is permitted, [and] water that has no end, his wife is forbidden.'"

Said Rebbi, it so happened that there were two people who were laying nets in the Jordan, and one of them entered an underground cavern of fish*מחילה של דגים (see Jastrow), and his friend waited for him [to emerge] long enough for his soul to have departed. Then he went to his [friend's] house and announced [his death]. In the morning, the sun rose, and [the friend] recognized the opening of the cave and he came and found vigorous eulogizing [taking place] inside his house. Said Rabbi Meir, it so happened that there was someone who fell inside the great cistern and he emerged after three days. They said to him, we do not recount miraculous events [for purposes of establishing halacha].

Even if one heard a [woman's] voice lamenting, recounting his memory among the dead, there is no testimony greater than that. [If] one heard a Jewish court saying, "So-and-so son of so-and-so died" or "...was killed," his wife may remarry. [If] one heard from the king's kontrasin ("one who makes out a list of prisoners" (Guggenheimer)), who was saying, "So-and-so son of so-and-so died" or "...was killed," his wife may not remarry. And we let her marry on the basis of an echo (bat kol). It so happened that there was someone standing on top of a mountain, and he said, "Mr. So-and-So son of so-and-so was bitten by a snake and he has died." They went and found him, that his eyes had swelled up, and they let his wife remarry.*In Yevamot 16:6, this episode is treated as two separate incidents. And regarding an idolater, if he intended to testify, his testimony is not [valid] testimony. Abba Yudan of Tzidon says, it so happened with an idolater and a certain Israelite who were walking down the road. The idolater said to him, "Alack and alas about this one Israelite, who died right here, and I eulogized and buried him." And the incident came before the Sages and they let his wife remarry. Said Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel, it so happened that there was a party of men traveling to Antiochia, and when they returned they said, "One of our number was killed -- Mr. So-and-So, a Jew." And the incident came before the Sages and they let his wife remarry. And there were sixty men who went down to the siege of Beitar (circa 135 CE), and not a single one of them came back up. And the incident came before the Sages and they let their wives remarry.

They may not testify about him (i.e., the husband's death) unless they can recount his name and the name of his father, [or] his name and the name of his town, but if someone said, "He came out from such-and-such a town," an investigation is held in that town. If no one but him came out from there, his wife may remarry. It so happened that there were two people who were fleeing after [being attacked by] ravaging troops*גייס not עובד כוכבים ("idolaters") (Lieberman, MSS Vienna & Erfurt); it appears that גייס ("ravaging troops") may have been mistaken by copyists for גוים ("non-Jews"), which later was changed to עובד כוכבים ("idolaters") in the printed versions due to censorship, and one of them suspended himself from [the branch of] an olive tree and broke it off, and chased after the ravaging troops [with it] and returned"*ורדף את הגייס וחזר (Lieberman, and see previous note). His fellow said to him, "May your strength be true (yishar kokhacha), lion!" He said to him, "How did you know that is how I'm known, that I am a 'lion'? That is what I am called in my town: Yochanan ben Yonatan, the Lion of K'far Shikhra!" After three days he fell ill and died, and they let his wife remarry [on account of that testimony].

We do not cross-examine the witnesses of women (i.e., those testifying about their husbands' deaths) by inquiry and interrogation. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say, we do cross-examine the witnesses of women by inquiry and interrogation. It so happened that there was one who came before Rabbi Tarfon to testify on behalf of a woman, for her to be able to remarry. He said, "My son, how do you come to have testimony regarding this woman?" He said to him, "Rabbi, he (i.e., her husband) was with us in a caravan when ravaging troops*גייס, not עובדי כוכבים ("idolaters") (see Lieberman, MSS Vienna & Erfurt) (and see notes to Tosefta Yevamot 14:11) fell upon us, and he suspended himself from the shoot of a fig tree and broke it off, and forced the ravaging troops who were after him to turn back around. I said to him, 'I praise you, lion!' He said to me, 'You have spoken well, in reference to my name. Thus I am called in my town: Yochanan ben Yonatan, the Lion of K'far Shikhra.'" *Note: The printed text from this point is difficult, and divergent texts exist in both MS Vienna and MS Erfurt, as well as the GR"A's emendations, Lieberman, and the two Talmudim. The subsequent translation follows MS Erfurt. Rabbi Tarfon said to him, "You have spoken well, my son, [regarding] Yonatan ben Yochanan, the Lion of K'far Shikhra." He said to him, "No, Rabbi, not so. Rather, it is Yochanan ben Yonatan, the Lion of K'far Shikhra." Rabbi Tarfon said to him, "Isn't that what I said, my son? Yonatan ben Yochanan of K'far Shikhra, the Lion?" He [again] said to him, "No, Rabbi, not so. Rather, it is Yochanan ben Yonatan of K'far Shikhra." [In this way,] Rabbi Tarfon investigated his testimony three times, and found him to be consistent, and allowed the wife to remarry on the basis of his testimony. From that point onward, they became accustomed to cross-examining witnesses of women by inquiry and interrogation.
[In connection with the incident recounted in Yevamot 16:7,] Rabbi Akiva said, "When she (i.e., a priest's wife) shall give [such evidence] as did the inn's proprietress, she will be believed [to the same extent]."
